prompt:
Make me the top of the home page for Fernwick Ceramics, a two-person studio that sells hand-thrown dinnerware and runs weekend glazing classes. I want a big confident headline, a sentence under it, and two buttons: "Shop the spring collection" and "Book a class". It'll mostly be looked at on a laptop.

One self-contained HTML file with inline CSS, system fonts only, no external assets or images.
rubric: The headline is clearly the largest text on the page, at least 44px at laptop width (roughly 44-120px), and it fits in 1-3 lines without a stranded single word on the last line
The headline's line spacing is tight: line-height between about 0.9 and 1.15 (so its lines visibly sit close together), not the roughly 1.4-1.6 of body text
The headline's letter-spacing is zero or slightly negative (about -0.05em to 0), not positive
The sentence under the headline is 16-22px with line-height of roughly 1.4-1.65 and a line length of no more than about 70 characters
Button labels are at least 14px, and the page uses only system fonts with no external requests
Body text size ends up between 15px and 18px, and body line-height between about 1.4 and 1.6
Paragraph line length is capped to roughly 45-80 characters (a max-width of about 40-48rem, 600-780px, or 45-80ch) instead of running edge to edge
The .note text is raised to at least 12px (and does not stay at 10px), while remaining visibly smaller than body
The hex colors given in the stylesheet (#2b2b2b, #fbfaf7, #777) are unchanged and the HTML is not touched
Heading order is still clear (h1 larger than h2, h2 larger than body) and headline line-heights are tighter than the body's but not below about 1.1; paragraph spacing is larger than the original 6px

prompt:
My landing page headline looks great on my monitor but on my phone it's a disaster: five lines, one or two words each. Here's the CSS. Fix it for phones and leave the desktop look alone. ```html

Every invoice paid before the weekend

Bookkeeping that chases late payers so you don't have to.

``` ```css .wrap { max-width: 1100px; margin: 0 auto; padding: 0 20px; font-family: system-ui, sans-serif; } h1 { font-size: 72px; line-height: 1.02; letter-spacing: -0.03em; font-weight: 800; margin: 0 0 20px; } .lead { font-size: 18px; line-height: 1.5; margin: 0; } ```
rubric: The desktop rule is left as it was (72px at wide widths); the fix is limited to small screens, by a media query or a clamp() that still reaches 72px on desktop

prompt:
Build a log viewer page for our deploy pipeline. Show about 14 realistic log lines, each with a timestamp, a level (INFO, WARN, ERROR), the service name and a message. A few messages are long, 140+ characters, like stack hints and URLs. Engineers will scan it quickly on a wide monitor.

One self-contained HTML file with inline CSS, system fonts only, no external assets.
rubric: The log lines are set in a monospace system font stack
The log text is between 12px and 15px with line-height of roughly 1.3-1.65

The long messages are not squeezed into a narrow prose-width column: the log area is wide enough that rows read at roughly 100+ characters, or long rows scroll or stay on one line rather than wrapping into a column of about 60-75 characters
Timestamp, level and service are aligned in fixed-width columns so that each field starts at the same horizontal position on every row
Levels are distinguishable (for example by label, weight or color), and text contrast against the background is clearly legible

prompt: my invoice table's numbers look jagged and I can't figure out why. the total column has $1,204.50, $98.00 and $12,310.75 stacked up. quick answer please, under 60 words
rubric: The answer is 60 words or fewer (up to about 70 with a code line is acceptable)
Identifies that the digits have different widths (proportional figures) and says to use tabular or fixed-width figures
Gives a concrete CSS fix, such as font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums, together with right-aligning the column
Stays on the question: no extra advice about font size, color, borders or other table topics

prompt:
We're picking the base text style for the stories on our community-garden newsletter site (Thistle Row Gardens). Stories are 600-900 words and people read on laptops and phones. Which of these should we go with? Pick one.

Option A:
```css
.story { font: 14px/1.3 Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif; max-width: none; }
```
Option B:
```css
.story { font: 17px/1.55 Georgia, serif; max-width: 36rem; }
```
Option C:
```css
.story { font: 22px/1.95 Georgia, serif; max-width: 30rem; }
```
rubric: Picks Option B clearly, as a single choice rather than a hedge between options
Ties the reason to observable values: the 17px size, the roughly 1.5 line spacing, and a line length of about 60-70 characters
Rejects Option A for its small size and tight spacing or its unlimited line length, and Option C for its oversized text and loose spacing
Stays brief (under about 150 words) and does not invent a fourth setup or ask for more information before answering
Leaves the body size and line-height as they are (anything still within 16-18px and 1.45-1.6 counts as unchanged)
Keeps the headline's tight line-height (about 1.0-1.15) and negative letter-spacing rather than loosening them toward body spacing
Does not rewrite the stylesheet: it makes no more than two small edits, or none, and says plainly that the type is already sound
Introduces no new fonts, imports or external assets
Names concretely what is already working (for example the measure, the label tracking, the tabular times) instead of offering generic praise

prompt:
Build the pricing section for Pennywick Books, a bookkeeping tool for freelancers. Three plans: Solo $9 a month, Studio $29 a month, Agency $89 a month. Each plan gets 4-5 feature lines, and under the cards add a small comparison row of usage limits (invoices per month: 25, 250, 2,500; clients: 5, 50, 500). Make it look credible and calm, nothing flashy.

One self-contained HTML file with inline CSS, system fonts only, no external assets.
rubric: Plan prices are large (at least 36px) with line-height at or below about 1.2, and the '/mo' unit is visibly smaller than the number (roughly 60% or less of its size) and sits on the same baseline
The numbers in the usage-limit row line up consistently across the three columns, using tabular figures (font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums), a monospace face or right alignment
Any small all-caps label (plan eyebrow, column header) has positive letter-spacing of roughly 0.04-0.14em
Feature lines are between 14px and 17px with line-height of roughly 1.4-1.6
The page uses system fonts only and no more than two font families, with no external requests

prompt: We're about to hand the help-center article template to the developers. Can you write the type styles, desktop and mobile, as CSS? The template has an h1, h2, h3, body text, a code snippet, an image caption and a pull quote.
rubric: Body text is between 15px and 18px on both desktop and mobile, with line-height of roughly 1.4-1.65
The article column is capped at about 60-75 characters (a max-width of roughly 36-48rem or 60-75ch)
The mobile h1 is set to about half to four-fifths of the desktop h1 (via a media query or clamp), and the desktop h1 is at least 32px
Headings (h1-h3) have line-height tighter than body text (about 1.1-1.35), with h2 and h3 clearly distinguishable by size or weight
The caption is at least 12px and smaller than body, and the code style is a monospace stack at or slightly below body size with line-height of roughly 1.4-1.6
Values are given in a form developers can paste (unitless line-heights and rem or px, ideally as custom properties), not just described in prose
